Beállítom A nationwide inspection program examining the entire operational chain of the battery industry in Hungary has been launched as of August 1, Minister of the Living Environment László Gajdos announced on Tuesday on his Facebook page . Gajdos wrote that battery manufacturing can only operate in Hungary under stringent official oversight, transparent regulations and genuine accountability, thereby ensuring acceptance by society. The inspections will extend to the plants’ actual capacity, materials used, emissions, water consumption, and waste management, as well as to the facilities related to battery production, solvents, and the management of industrial waste, according to MTI. According to the minister, the inspections will go beyond simply reviewing the submitted documents: the authorities will compare the data in the permits with the actual operations on-site and will inspect the entire process, covering everything from the route of the raw materials, through emissions, to waste management. Where warranted, the authorities will collect samples and conduct laboratory tests; serious violations or hazards will result in immediate regulatory action. According to Gajdos, the program’s goal is to identify and eliminate violations, as well as to tighten regulations, licensing practices, and official inspections. “I consider the health and safety of the Hungarian people and the protection of natural resources and the environment as my top priority,” the minister wrote in his post. The Tisza government announced in early June that it was working on setting up an autonomous national environmental protection authority and that a nationwide inspection program would be launched at industrial facilities which pose the greatest environmental risk. It was also announced at that time that a nationwide plan for inspecting battery plants and other hazardous facilities would be finalized by the end of June, and that the regulation under which the locations of battery recycling plants could be designated by ministerial decision would be repealed. The goal is to ensure that, in the future, such investments are made based on uniform and transparent rules rather than on individual political decisions. Along with the automotive industry, the previous, Fidesz-led government saw the battery industry as a potential pillar of Hungary’s economic growth. In line with this, over the past decade, it provided substantial government subsidies and offered an extraordinarily favourable regulatory and administrative environment for the sector. This attracted the world’s largest battery manufacturers to the country, and even the repeated protests of locals in the affected towns couldn’t prevent the construction of the multiple plants involved in battery production. Zsolt Tárkányi, a representative of the Tisza Party in Parliament and the Parliamentary State Secretary of the Ministry of Transportation and Investment, previously said that a new authority—which will oversee the operations of battery factories and other key industrial facilities—could be established by September. According to the plans, in the event of serious violations, this authority will be authorised to impose fines amounting to billions of forints on the companies involved; furthermore, in extreme cases, it will be authorized to revoke all of their operating permits, which would effectively mean shutting them down. The operation of a Chinese-owned battery plant in Debrecen was recently suspended due to serious environmental concerns. This spring, Telex reported on the previous government's cover-up of the serious occupational safety violations at the Samsung SDI factory in Göd. We previously also reported on the hidden hazards of waste handling in Hungary's battery boom. https://www.thetelegraphandargus.co.uk/n.text: Court Crime Bradford Man sentenced for sending threatening message to councillor By Sam Reed T&A Reporter Share 0 Comments 2 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A MAN has been sentenced for sending a threatening social media message to a Bradford councillor. Grzegorz Grzech, 37, of Beech Crescent in Undercliffe, appeared before Bradford Magistrates’ Court earlier this month, where he admitted to sending a message to Councillor Susan Fricker (Labour, Bingley East) in which he threatened that she would soon be hanged from a tree. On Friday, he was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Magistrates also imposed a restraining order for an indefinite period which prevents Grzech from approaching or contacting Cllr Fricker either in person or on social media. Nadine Clough, prosecuting, read a section of the victim impact statement from Cllr Fricker to the court. Councillor Susan Fricker at an election count in May (Image: T&A) It said she was due to attend two public events in Bingley shortly after receiving the messages. The victim statement said: "I felt quite terrified to attend due to the worry there could be someone planning to do something to me. "This affected me throughout those events, and ever since when I am out in public. "I shouldn’t have to go to event feeling frightened that I might be harmed." What was the message Last October, Grzech used his Facebook Messenger account to send Cllr Fricker an image of a tree with numerous dead bodies hanging from it. The image was followed with a message which read: "One day it will be you on that tree." What happened at the latest hearing? Grzech appeared before the court wearing a grey jacket and a gold watch and was assisted by a Polish interpreter. A section of the pre-sentence report prepared by the Probation Service was read to the court. It revealed that Grzech had taken exception to social media posts made by Cllr Fricker in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The chair of the magistrates' bench told Grzech that his response had been disproportionate. 'Entirely out of character' In mitigation, it was said Grzech was "entirely shameful and remorseful" for his actions and that the incident was "entirely out of character". The court also heard that Grzech's mother has health and mobility issues and is reliant on her son. 'A really serious offence' Passing sentence, the chair said: "This is a really serious offence. You just can't send those sorts of messages. "You've had a real impact on this councillor." The magistrates took into account Grzech's previous good character and early guilty plea when passing sentence. He is also required to undertake 10 rehabilitation activity requirement days and an unpaid work requirement. Response from Councillor Fricker Responding to the sentencing, Cllr Fricker said: "This has been a very distressing experience for me and my family and I am relieved that it is now ended. "I'm grateful to the police and the Crown Prosecution Service for taking appropriate action. "The defendant pleaded guilty at the first opportunity ensuring that this has now been dealt with. "It's clear from the sentence given by the magistrates that they recognised the seriousness of the offence, it's really important that elected representatives are able to carry out their duties and responsibilities without fear or favour. "I shall continue to do my best to serve Bingley and the Bradford District, to support and serve the community that elected me." Why it was important to report the post to police Following Grzech’s guilty plea earlier this month, Cllr Fricker told the T&A she felt it was important to report the matter to "push back" against an increasingly hostile climate for politicians. She said: "After significant distress and anxious thought I decided to report it to the police, I found the situation extremely difficult to deal with but I concluded that I needed to report it not only for the safety of myself and my family but also with a sense of wider responsibility as a politician to push back against what seems to be an increasingly dangerous and hostile climate for politicians. "I am deeply concerned about the impact online abuse is having on our politics and our society. "It is my hope that by reporting it and a prosecution taking place it will act as a deterrent to others and will, I hope, cause people to think more carefully about the way they express themselves online and generally, in this case about a public servant." Photograph: Ukrainian military general staff View image in fullscreen Remains of a workshop at the Kamensky Combine, a Russian rocket fuel and gunpowder manufacturer in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov region, Russia. Photograph: Ukrainian military general staff Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russian campaign to ‘weaponise winter’ under way Ukrainian energy companies Naftogaz and DTEK report string of attacks; pictures show success of strike on Russian rocket fuel maker. What we know on day 1,637 Warren Murray and agencies Mon 17 Aug 2026 20.58 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 21.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian drones and missiles attacked facilities of Ukraine’s Naftogaz energy company 13 times over the past week and Moscow has targeted its premises almost 300 times since the start of the year, the state energy company said. The latest attacks caused serious damage to equipment and production capacity but no injuries. Ukrainian officials say Russia is “weaponising” the coming winter . DTEK, a coal mining and power production company, said a Russian attack started a fire at one of its mines, killing a 52-year-old man. Russian organisers have cancelled an “international” military music festival due to be held in Red Square from Friday . After Ukraine attacked Russia with a record number of drones , organisers of the Spasskaya Tower festival said it was being postponed until next year. More drones attacked Moscow over Monday night, Russian authorities reported. Flights had to be suspended at the capital’s airports of Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky, said Rosaviatsia, the Russian aviation agency. Ukraine’s military general staff released pictures of the results after a strike operation blew up rocket fuel and explosives workshops in Russia’s Rostov region . The strike on the night of 16 August hit the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, destroying two workshops and damaging four more. “The Kamensky Combine is a Russian military-industrial complex enterprise that produces solid rocket fuel for the munitions of the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), as well as for a range of missile systems and air-delivered munitions.” A Russian drone crashed and exploded in Moldova , Ukrainian authorities said. The Institute for the Study of War said it was reportedly a Russian Banderol, a winged cruise missile cum loitering munition. Moldova, which borders Ukraine, condemned the violation ⁠of its airspace. The craft entered Moldovan airspace on Monday afternoon, came down and exploded near the settlement of Talmaza, setting grass on fire but leaving no casualties according to local authorities. As Vladimir Putin prepares to cement his rule with stage-managed elections in September, a court has given a senior Russian opposition politician 11 years and one month in prison for speaking out against the war . The jailing of Lev Shlosberg comes soon after the Yabloko party to which he belongs was banned from the elections. In a separate ruling on Monday, Russia’s supreme court denied Yabloko’s appeal against the ban. Yabloko – the Russian word for apple – had been the only official political party on the ballot that overtly opposes the war. Shlosberg addressed the court , saying that for 30 years, Russia has travelled “a path from hopes for freedom to the almost complete destruction of human and civil rights and freedoms”. The war in Ukraine had “changed the lives of every Russian citizen without exception” and once its true death toll became known “the entire country will shudder”. Yabloko said Shlosberg would appeal against the “barbaric sentence” he had received. The party declared he was being punished for “love of the motherland and calls for a ceasefire”. Amnesty International denounced the verdict. “His arbitrary prosecution and sentencing are blatant reprisals for exercising his right to freedom of expression to call for peace,” said Marie Struthers, Amnesty eastern Europe and central Asia director. Yabloko’s chairman, Nikolai Rybakov, said the party would continue its fight by lodging a complaint to the presidium of the supreme court and possibly the constitutional court. “We achieved the main thing: the whole world knows how many people in Russia want peace , want to live normally and to raise children under a peaceful sky in their country,” Rybakov said. Regarding Shlosberg’s sentence, Rybakov said “our feelings are with Lev and other political prisoners who have fought and are fighting for peace, for people to not die”. Russia sought to threaten Britain with “consequences” over reports that British drones including a stealth model were used to strike targets on Russia’s mainland . Ukraine used drones made by two UK companies for deep strikes, the Sunday Times reported (paywall) . The story cited a UK defence source as saying: “Russia has been very effective at keeping the west nervous about hitting it too hard. These attacks mean the UK is effectively signalling to Russia and our allies that we’re not [nervous] any more .” Analysts and supporters of Ukraine have complained throughout the war about Kyiv’s western backers exhibiting “reflexive control” – hesitating to support Ukraine’s military in case Moscow might somehow retaliate. https://www.newyorker.com/news/global-no.text: I checked in with Barber in the weeks after Donald Trump’s shock electoral victory in November, 2016, which was being celebrated by a decidedly anti-cosmopolitan crowd in the United States and Europe. Barber died half a year later, of pancreatic cancer, but he was still buoyant and optimistic when we spoke, his idealism intact. “These reactionaries are the last wave in a series of political attempts to pretend that sovereign states still work,” he told me, adding that “the right-wing nationalism of the Trumps will become not so much toxic obstacles to history but an increasingly obsolete expression.” It’s taking a while for him to be proved right. Far from obsolete, right-wing nationalism is ubiquitous on the global scene; in many places, it is on the ascendance. Trump may be in his final years in office, but “America First” is stamped all over international politics: European leaders extoll the need to build up national militaries; industrial policy and tariffs are the order of the day; countries everywhere are finding their interdependencies—their reliance on global supply chains, their exposure to powerful neighbors—to be a source of vulnerability, not strength. In Europe, multiethnic capitals are pilloried by the far right as demographic time bombs, ground zero for invasions of unwanted foreigners. In the United States, meanwhile, cities have come under siege by federal authorities carrying out sweeping anti-migrant raids. If cities aren’t universally seen as the engines of progress that Barber believed them to be, they are, in an angry age, bastions of defiance. Mayors may not be close to “ruling” the world, but they are often defending and defining a liberal version of it. After Minneapolis withstood and, in large part, rallied against a major incursion by ICE and other federal agencies, the city’s mayor, Jacob Frey, hailed a spirit of resistance that he saw reinforcing a civic ideal. “Some would like to define America as a nation that is made possible by the people who we keep out,” he said earlier this year, at an event in Washington, D.C., where he received an award from the nonprofit group Refugees International. But, he insisted, “America is made possible by the people we invite in.” Other mayors, including some far from the United States, have echoed that sentiment. Henriette Reker, who served two terms as the mayor of Cologne, Germany, until last year, survived an assassination attempt, in 2015, by a far-right assailant angry about migration. Reker spent years in her role thereafter enduring death threats for her support of asylum seekers. “Cologne has been accepting people who have come to the city for thousands of years,” Reker recently told the PBS show “Open Mind,” which is running a series on mayors from across the globe. “People from all over the world come here to trade and stay here. This is a coöperation that has worked well and will continue to work well in the future.” Two of the other mayors interviewed for “Open Mind”—New York City’s Zohran Mamdani and Toronto’s Olivia Chow—met earlier this month in Manhattan, as more than two dozen municipal leaders convened for a summit called the Urban20, which was staged in parallel to the high-level meetings at the United Nations General Assembly. Mamdani and Chow swapped notes on dealing with the constraints placed on them by their state and provincial governors, and on their respective battles over renters’ rights and the high costs of living in their cities. “Sometimes the relationship between our national governments is a little more complicated than we like,” Chow said, referring to the ongoing dispute between Trump and the Canadian Prime Minister, Mark Carney. “But friendship between cities doesn’t need permission from our capitals. We can just do it.” Mamdani pointed to a burgeoning solidarity. “Global challenges cannot be faced in isolation,” he said during closing remarks for the summit. “The vision of coexistence that our cities so proudly model is evidence of that very point.” He also gave the mayors of Barcelona, Helsinki, and Rome a tour of a wastewater-treatment plant in the Bronx, insisting on the importance of delivering good governance and getting basic things done. Mamdani has described his approach as “sewer socialism,” using the resources and the tools he has to improve public infrastructure and the conditions of the city. He believes mayors, whatever their politics, have to identify and focus attention on what they can tangibly make better. Otherwise, speaking for his own part and referring to how his Republican opponents tend to talk about the failings of cities run by Democrats, he said, “If you are staring at an example of social disorder or social inefficiency, and the left refuses to explain either why it has happened or how they will fix it, then the right gets to point at someone in the immediate area and say, ‘That’s who did it.’ ” New York City’s mayor may be America’s most obvious example of a metropolitan leader who stands in contrast to his country’s nationalist politics, but he’s hardly alone. Last week, even as Germany’s far right racked up new successes in state elections, voters in Berlin delivered victory to the leftist Die Linke party, led by Elif Eralp, a forty-five-year-old lawyer of Turkish descent whom many are already calling “Germany’s Mamdani.” She’s now the top contender to lead the city’s government, pending coalition talks, and has centered her campaign on making the German capital more affordable, including through a controversial scheme to expropriate tens of thousands of apartments from private real-estate companies seen as responsible for Berlin’s high rents. “This city belongs to all of us, not to the speculators,” Eralp said in a recent speech. Her designs may set up a showdown with the German Chancellor, the center-right Friedrich Merz, who opposes the plan to socialize housing. Mayors are, of course, limited in what they can do. They can speak in transcendent terms, but they can’t transcend the checks of state and federal power, or the budgetary controls that, in many instances, narrow their scope for action. But their ability to competently run a city, connecting directly with local needs, often sets them up for national politics. The new British Prime Minister, the Labour politician Andy Burnham, honed a sunny, folksy brand of center-left politics for almost a decade as the mayor of Manchester; supporters hope that his broadly successful legacy there can help revive his floundering party. To date, the most serious challenge to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s increasingly autocratic tenure came from Ekrem İmamoğlu, the popular mayor of Istanbul. But İmamoğlu has been detained, since 2025, on a string of charges of corruption and bribery which are widely believed to be trumped up and designed to bar him from ever competing against Erdoğan nationally. An alphabet soup of networks and alliances brings together scores of cities into various political campaigns—these include entities such as the C40, which involves dozens of mayors from around the world acting together on climate policies, and the urban alliance for gun safety set up by the former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg which coördinates anti-gun policy among hundreds of U.S. cities, and the Mayors Migration Council, which brings together Western mayors reckoning with influxes of undocumented migrants alongside mayors in the developing world who administer cities overwhelmed by internal displacements and climate refugees. The Pact of Free Cities, founded in 2019, began with four members—the capital cities of Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia—and styled itself in deliberate opposition to the illiberal populists who held national power in Central Europe. There are now forty-five members, including ten American cities. Last year, I spoke with one of the group’s leaders, Gergely Karácsony, the left-leaning mayor of Budapest, who was elected in 2019, and often came into conflict with Hungary’s then Prime Minister, the right-wing nationalist Viktor Orbán. “Thirty years ago, when our countries cast off communist dictatorship, we hoped that a new era had dawned for the peoples of Europe—an era of freedom, peace, rationality, and cooperation. Today, those ideals are being upheld by cities, as islands in a political climate that seeks once again to concentrate all power at the center,” Karácsony told me, talking about the ways that Budapest was trying to buttress civil society, defending the city’s L.G.B.T.Q.+ community and Hungary’s beleaguered independent media. This spring, those efforts bore indirect fruit. Orbán was finally defeated, in a landslide, by a united opposition, which is in the process of rehabilitating democratic institutions that were warped by almost two decades that he was in power. “I believe Budapest was necessary for all of this,” Káracsony told a journalist in Slovakia, explaining that “the democratic commitments of society, the belief in social cohesion, were able to survive and return to national politics” because they had endured in the capital. In the same interview, though, he acknowledged that alliances of mayors may not be able to thwart the rise of the far right in many Western democracies. “Something has gone off the rails, and the current form of globalization is devouring democracy,” he said, in language Barber would have found familiar. “Either democracy will humanize globalization, or globalization will destroy democracy.” ♦
